:::{#thm-det-diagonal}
#### Determinant of a diagonal matrix

The determinant (@def-determinant) of a $p \times p$ diagonal matrix
(@def-diagonal-matrix)
is the product of its diagonal entries:

$$
\det\paren{
\begin{bmatrix}
d_1    & \cdots & 0      \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0      & \cdots & d_p
\end{bmatrix}
} = \prod_{i=1}^p d_i
$$

:::

::: proof

By [induction](proof-writing.qmd#def-proof-by-induction) on $p$.
For $p = 1$, the matrix is $\begin{bmatrix} d_1 \end{bmatrix}$,
and its determinant is $d_1$ by definition.

For $p \ge 2$, suppose the result holds for $(p-1) \times (p-1)$ diagonal matrices,
and let $\matr{D}$ be $p \times p$ and diagonal.
Row 1 of $\matr{D}$ is $(d_1, 0, \ldots, 0)$,
so only the $j = 1$ term of the definition can be nonzero,
and deleting row 1 and column 1 of $\matr{D}$
leaves the diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $d_2, \ldots, d_p$:

$$
\ba
\det(\matr{D})
&= (-1)^{1+1}\, d_1 \det\paren{\matr{D}_{(11)}}
 + \sum_{j=2}^p (-1)^{1+j} \cd 0 \cd \det\paren{\matr{D}_{(1j)}}
&& \text{(definition)}
\\
&= d_1 \det\paren{\matr{D}_{(11)}}
&& \text{(drop the zero terms)}
\\
&= d_1 \prod_{i=2}^p d_i
&& \text{(induction hypothesis)}
\\
&= \prod_{i=1}^p d_i
&& \text{(combine)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-det-diagonal}
#### Determinant of a scaled identity matrix

For a number $c$,
$c\,\matr{I}_p$ is diagonal with every diagonal entry equal to $c$,
so $\det(c\,\matr{I}_p) = c^p$.
In particular, $\det(\matr{I}_p) = 1$.

:::
